Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Vignette:
At sixty-two, the night his daughter, Elara, was admitted with acute bacterial meningitis had never truly left him. Quan remembered the stark white corridor of the pediatric intensive care unit, the steady hum of ventilation pumps, and the way the attending physician had calmly explained the sequence of intubation. He stood beside her bedside, watching the medical team adjust the endotracheal tube, his own breath catching as Elara’s small chest hitched with the mechanical rhythm. He had come to believe that if he had only known more, the airway could have stayed clear. The antiseptic sting of the chlorhexidine wipes had clung to his jacket. That scent, the medical equipment, and the sight of procedures would later align in his awareness. For months after she recovered, the memory refused to settle in the past. When he tried to describe that night to his late wife, to her sister, or even to his therapist, he would begin with the monitor’s alarm, then his hands would start to tremble, and he would lose the thread, unable to finish the sentence. The image simply kept playing behind his eyelids, frame by frame, as though the clock had stopped turning. Over the years, these sensations and the quiet guilt that accompanied them began to shape his daily rhythm. He stopped attending neighborhood baby showers, steering clear of the cribs and the cooing infants. He avoided pediatric clinics for his grandchildren, citing work commitments, and found himself walking past hospitals in the opposite direction. He did not know why his pulse would suddenly spike or why his shoulders would lock when a child wheezed on the street, but he learned to pace his life around these moments. He told himself this was merely prudent, choosing routes that bypassed medical centers, selecting hand sanitizers with citrus over clinical formulations, and declining any medical procedure beyond the bare minimum. The negative emotions and the physical tension existed side by side, occupying different hours of his day, while the memories played out in the quiet spaces between appointments. Now, at seventy-five, Quan sat at his standing desk in the spare bedroom that served as his cybersecurity command center. The dual monitors glowed with network traffic logs, each blinking node a data packet waiting to be analyzed. He spent decades mapping digital vulnerabilities, training his mind to anticipate breaches. Yet on a Tuesday morning last week, while reviewing a healthcare client’s server logs, the office assistant had walked in with a bottle of industrial-grade hand sanitizer. The sharp, antiseptic vapor cut through the room, and his vision blurred for a second. He was certain the room was tilting, certain that the rhythmic beep of his wristwatch was morphing into the high-pitched alarm of a cardiac monitor. He had to excuse himself, pacing the hallway until the dizziness passed, his breath coming in shallow draws. The avoidance and the physical reactions had coexisted for years, but this particular trigger had cracked through his routine; he missed critical updates, skipped team briefings, and found himself unable to articulate the source of his distress to his own daughter. What finally brought him to the clinic was not a single crisis, but a quiet accumulation of broken routines. He had come to believe that his mind was no longer a secure system he could patch from the inside. He sat now on the edge of the intake chair, his hands resting heavily on his knees, wondering if he could ever stop bracing for a threat that had already passed. He wanted to understand why the past felt so present, and whether he might one day sit in a room with a baby’s mobile spinning overhead without feeling the floor drop away.
